title: Token-synchronous memory: decode sweeps restore every row each token
idea: Align the workload clock with the leakage clock: LLM decode reads all dense weights and active KV each token (~20-50 ms) and every DRAM read restores its row, so the refresh engine is removed from the die; a 1-bit-per-row coverage bitmap faults if any row goes unread for one retention window, and sparse MoE experts live in an NV tier.
why: Zero refresh power and 10-20% of bandwidth returned (fact 3); refresh counters and logic leave the periphery (fact 7).

title: Smoke detector: leaky analog charge counters catch row hammer
idea: Smoke builds up in an ionization chamber until the alarm trips. Give each group of 4 rows one tiny capacitor in the wordline-driver strip that gets a fixed charge packet per activation and leaks with a ~64 ms time constant; a comparator trips at ~500 activations' worth of charge and queues a targeted neighbour refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9, ~1k activation threshold): replaces SRAM counter tables and TRR logic with ~3 transistors plus 1 cap per 4 rows, monitors every row so it cannot be evaded by many-sided patterns, and costs <1% die.

title: Venetian blinds: bit-plane layout fetches only requested precision bits
idea: Tilt Venetian blinds to let in only the light you want. Store tensors transposed into bit-planes across column groups, with a precision-select field in the column command so a 4-bit or 8-bit inference read opens only those planes' micro-rows and moves only those bits, not the full 16-bit words.
why: Activation plus transfer energy scales with bits actually needed: 2-4x from precision alone, and >10x when combined with micro-row activation that already removes overfetch.

title: Gigahertz CCD loops: one floating-diffusion amp per 64 bits
idea: Failure mined: 1970s CCD memories (Fairchild, Intel 2416) lost to DRAM on millisecond serial latency and charge-transfer loss. Fix: 64-stage buried-channel CCD loops with imaging-grade transfer efficiency (>99.9999%), 2-phase clocked at 4 GHz (worst-case 16 ns rotation), each sensed and re-injected by one floating-diffusion amplifier. Packets hold 2 bits (4 charge levels), and there are no per-bit contacts, capacitors or wordline drivers.
why: 10x at the same cost: ~2F^2 per packet vs 6F^2 (3x) x 2 bits per packet (2x) x periphery shrinking from 49% to ~10% (~1.7x) = ~10x. Built with CMOS-image-sensor masks (no capacitor module, little EUV) in U.S. image-sensor fabs.
note: Revives CCD loops with CIS-grade transfer; clocking every gate at 4 GHz costs huge CV^2f power, and GHz transfer efficiency is unproven.

title: Charge-injection-device cells: two-gate X-Y charge storage with non-destructive reads
idea: Failure mined: GE's charge-injection device (CID) imager lost to CCDs, yet it had an X-Y addressed, transistor-free pixel of two coupled MOS gates, read non-destructively by moving charge between the gates and sensing the column. Fix: use CID pairs as memory cells, with the row gate and column gate overlapping one storage well. A write injects charge; a read shifts it under the column gate and back, so the charge never leaves the well and can be re-read for multi-level sensing.
why: 10x at the same cost: a transistor-free ~4F^2 cell (1.5x) x 3 bits per well from averaged non-destructive re-reads (3x) x no restore and much less periphery (~2x) = ~9-10x, using planar CMOS-image-sensor processing.
note: Transistor-free X-Y well with nondestructive re-reads; doubt: thermal generation fills wells fast and column signal is tiny.

title: Matchstick: consume-once reads with decoupled sense amps skip restore
idea: A match is used once: add an isolation gate so the SA latches from a +/-100 mV bitline signal without driving the bitline rail to rail, and add a READ-CONSUME command; for data the host marks read-once (streamed KV cache, network buffers, transpose scratch) the row is left destroyed and marked free, so neither full swing nor restore happens.
why: Full-swing restore is >70% of activation energy; consume reads cut array energy ~10x and halve tRAS; needs a JEDEC/CXL command and OS tracking of dead rows.

title: Gleaner's cool tier: sense-marginal dies for liquid-cooled racks
idea: Farmers glean the field after harvest. Dies that fail sense margin only above ~75 C are binned as cool-tier DDR5/HBM, sold at standard JEDEC timings into liquid- and immersion-cooled racks that hold devices under 60 C.
why: Turns marginal yield loss into salable bits (+3-8% supply), exploiting how leakage and offset tighten when cool (fact 3).

title: Saprotroph recycling: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Saprotrophic fungi turn dead wood into new growth. An FPGA CXL Type-3 card hosts 8-16 salvaged DDR4 RDIMMs from retired servers and takes over the aged chips' 'periphery intelligence': per-DIMM retention profiling, chipkill ECC, adaptive refresh and bad-row remap, so they serve as a slower tier. One board spin plus firmware, ~$800k in 24 months, with revenue from refurbished pools.
why: Supply axis: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Reusing even 10% adds memory at ~10-20% of new DDR5 cost/bit with zero fab capex.

title: Tire retreading: CXL rehab buffer gives retired DRAM second life
idea: Truck fleets retread tires instead of buying new. Sell a CXL memory-expander buffer chip whose periphery profiles retired DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs in situ (per-row retention margin, weak-column sensing), applies per-region refresh rates and column remaps, and pools them as tier-2 memory under strong ECC, fed by hyperscaler decommissioning streams.
why: Water/supply: a reused GB avoids essentially all of its manufacturing water (>10x vs new) and adds supply with no fab; large volumes of retired DRAM are shredded today.

title: Erasure-flagging sense amps: weak decisions marked, not guessed
idea: Limit: accept a raw bit error rate of 1e-4. A second, time-delayed sample in each SA flags bits that resolved slowly (small |dV|) as erasures, and a short per-burst erasure code corrects up to 4 flagged bits per 64 B with little overhead, since known-location errors cost half the parity.
why: Sense margin: tolerating 1e-4 lets Cs shrink ~30% or refresh intervals lengthen 2-4x (facts 1, 3), with soft information borrowed from NAND applied to DRAM.
note: Slow-resolving SA bits flagged as erasures double what ECC can correct; this is NAND soft info applied to DRAM.

title: Electron-beam-addressed charge film (EBAM) with field-emitter arrays
idea: Failure mined: 1970s EBAM/BEAMOS (GE, Control Data) stored bits as charge written and read by an electron beam on a MOS target, and died on vacuum, beam deflection and slow serial access. Fix: replace the deflected beam with a CMOS-driven Spindt field-emitter array in which each tip covers a 64x64 patch at 8 nm spot pitch through a small electrostatic microlens. Bits are charge in a nitride film, read by beam-induced current to a common backplate.
why: 10x at the same cost: no per-bit access transistor, wordline or bitline. An 8 nm bit pitch on an unpatterned film is ~13x DRAM density, and the only patterning is the emitter array at a relaxed ~200 nm pitch (no EUV).
note: Transistor-free 8 nm-pitch charge film could beat DRAM density ~13x; doubts: 8 nm spots via microlenses, vacuum packaging, nitride endurance, serial access latency.

title: Blessing in disguise: Geiger-mode avalanche bitline sensing of 100-electron cells
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise turns breakdown, normally a failure, into gain: each bitline segment ends in a SPAD-like junction biased just above avalanche breakdown, which a stored packet of ~100 electrons triggers into a full-swing self-quenched pulse, so storage nodes need only ~0.02 fF and can be plain planar diffusions.
why: 100x path: deletes the capacitor module (Fact 1) and allows near-4F2 planar or stacked cells on mature nodes; trade-offs: dark counts and afterpulsing need repeat reads and strong ECC, ~10-100 ns quench recovery and higher sense voltage. Attacks Facts 1, 2 and 4.
note: Avalanche gain could delete the capacitor module; doubts are dark counts, afterpulsing, high bias at DRAM pitch, junction leakage swamping 100-electron packets.
